questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman has well-demarcated, salmon-colored plaques with silvery scale on both elbows and knees. The clinician gently picks the scale off one plaque. Which of the following findings, if seen, best distinguishes her condition from other scaly skin disorders?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central clearing with an active border

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dry white flakes with no bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greasy yellow scale beneath the plaque

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pinpoint bleeding points on the base

explanation.summary: Pinpoint bleeding when psoriatic scale is removed (Auspitz sign) distinguishes psoriasis from other scaly disorders.
explanation.whyCorrect: This is the Auspitz sign: small pinpoint bleeding areas appear when psoriatic scales are picked off. The lecture notes it helps separate psoriasis from other scaly disorders, which do not bleed when picked.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central clearing is not a psoriasis sign; psoriatic plaques are uniformly scaly with a well-defined border.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A dry, non-bleeding base is what other scaly diseases show; psoriasis bleeds at pinpoint sites.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Greasy scale is not the finding the lecture describes on removing psoriatic scale; psoriatic scale is silvery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pus streaks are not seen when ordinary plaque scale is removed.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man with no prior skin disease develops, over 3 days, dozens of 3-8 mm pink scaly papules scattered over his trunk and upper arms. Three weeks earlier he had fever and a painful throat with tonsillar exudate. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A sudden eruption of many sub-centimeter scaly papules on the trunk after strep pharyngitis is guttate psoriasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Guttate psoriasis is the sudden appearance of many small papules and plaques under 1 cm, mostly on the trunk and proximal extremities, in young adults with no psoriasis history. It is typically associated with a prior streptococcal pharyngitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythrodermic psoriasis covers the entire skin surface, red and scaly from head to toe.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Generalized pustular psoriasis presents with sheets of erythema and superficial pustules with systemic toxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inverse psoriasis involves intertriginous areas such as the groin and axillae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plaque psoriasis forms 1-10 cm plaques on extensor surfaces, not a sudden shower of sub-centimeter papules.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman with long-standing psoriasis completed a 10-day course of oral prednisone for an asthma flare. Four days after the last dose she develops fever, chills, and myalgias, with abrupt widespread erythema studded with superficial pustules. Which of the following agents is the targeted therapy for this condition?

explanation.summary: Generalized pustular psoriasis, often after systemic steroid withdrawal, is treated with the IL-36 receptor antibody spesolimab.
explanation.whyCorrect: Withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids can trigger generalized pustular psoriasis (von Zumbusch), a life-threatening acute form. The lecture states it is treated with spesolimab, a monoclonal antibody antagonistic to the IL-36 receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Apremilast is an oral phosphodiesterase inhibitor and not the treatment the lecture gives for this emergency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated in psoriasis; their withdrawal caused this flare.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Secukinumab is an IL-17 antibody for plaque psoriasis; the lecture names spesolimab for pustular psoriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ustekinumab blocks IL-12/23 and is used for psoriasis generally, not as the targeted pustular agent.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man asks why his plaques form. His dermatologist explains that activated dendritic cells in his skin release a cytokine that drives the differentiation and maintenance of a T-helper subset, which then releases cytokines that make keratinocytes proliferate. Which cytokine do the dendritic cells release?

explanation.summary: Dendritic cells make IL-23, which sustains Th17 cells, the central axis of psoriasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Psoriasis is driven primarily by dendritic cell activation and the IL-23/Th17 axis. Dendritic cells produce IL-23, which promotes the differentiation and maintenance of Th17 cells; Th17 cells then release IL-17 and IL-22.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IL-4 is not part of the IL-23/Th17 axis that the lecture describes as driving psoriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-5 is not among the cytokines the lecture names in psoriasis pathogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-10 is not described as driving psoriatic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-13 is not part of the dendritic cell-Th17 pathway of psoriasis.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man has scaly plaques over the lumbosacral area and intergluteal cleft. Because seborrheic dermatitis and cutaneous lupus are on the differential, a biopsy is done. It shows epidermal thickening, nuclei retained in the stratum corneum, elongated rete pegs, and clusters of neutrophils in the upper epidermis. Which epidermal layer is characteristically absent?

explanation.summary: Psoriasis histology shows absence of the stratum granulosum along with parakeratosis and acanthosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The epidermal changes of psoriasis include parakeratosis, acanthosis, absence of the stratum granulosum, and thickening of the stratum spinosum that elongates the rete pegs, with Munro microabscesses of neutrophils.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The basal layer is present in psoriasis; its loss is not part of the described histology.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stratum corneum is present and parakeratotic, retaining nuclei.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of this layer is not one of the psoriasis findings the lecture lists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The stratum spinosum is thickened in psoriasis, not absent.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has 3 months of a painful, swollen right knee and left ankle with morning stiffness. He has active scaly plaques on his elbows. His nails, digits, and hand radiographs are normal, and no relative has skin disease. Which additional finding would, by itself, allow him to meet the CASPAR classification for psoriatic arthritis?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Additional itchy plaques on the scalp

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pain at the Achilles tendon insertion

explanation.summary: Under CASPAR, current psoriasis (2 points) plus a negative rheumatoid factor (1 point) meets the 3-point threshold.
explanation.whyCorrect: CASPAR requires inflammatory articular disease plus at least 3 points. Current psoriasis scores 2 points; a negative rheumatoid factor adds 1, reaching 3. Nail dystrophy, dactylitis, family history, and juxta-articular new bone are excluded by the stem.

whyWrongByChoice.B: More current psoriasis does not add beyond the 2 points he already has.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inflammatory markers are not a CASPAR criterion and add no points.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spinal disease is another form of the entry articular disease, not a scoring item.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enthesitis counts as the required inflammatory articular disease, which he already has; it scores no points.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has psoriasis covering 12% of her body surface, swollen distal finger joints, and a sausage-shaped toe. She also has ulcerative colitis with recurrent flares. She wants one systemic agent that will help her skin, joints, and gut. Which of the following is the best choice?

explanation.summary: In psoriasis with IBD, choose an IL-23 inhibitor; avoid IL-17 inhibitors, which list IBD as an adverse event.
explanation.whyCorrect: Psoriasis and IBD share IL-23-mediated pathways, and the IL-23 inhibitors treat both psoriasis and IBD. Guselkumab is an IL-23 monoclonal antibody, a reasonable single agent for psoriasis with arthritis and colitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acitretin is an oral retinoid that does not treat inflammatory bowel disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Brodalumab is an IL-17 antibody, and IBD is among its listed adverse events.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ixekizumab is an IL-17 antibody, a class that can cause or worsen inflammatory bowel disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Secukinumab is an IL-17 antibody; inflammatory bowel disease is a listed adverse event of IL-17 blockade.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man has three well-demarcated plaques with silvery scale on his elbows and one knee; together they cover an area about the size of two of his palms. He has no joint symptoms or nail changes. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

explanation.summary: Psoriasis covering 5% or less of BSA (1 palm = 1%) is limited and is treated topically.
explanation.whyCorrect: One palm is about 1% of body surface area, so he has about 2% BSA, which is limited disease (moderate-to-severe is greater than 5%). Limited disease is treated topically, such as a topical corticosteroid with or without a vitamin D analog like calcipotriene.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Systemic corticosteroids are contraindicated in psoriasis because withdrawal can trigger pustular psoriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cyclosporine is an oral systemic agent with renal and blood pressure toxicity, not for limited disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Biologics are for moderate-to-severe disease or psoriatic arthritis, neither of which he has.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Methotrexate is a systemic agent for moderate-to-severe disease, with organ toxicity risks.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman with moderate-to-severe psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis is about to begin adalimumab. Which of the following must be done before the first dose?

explanation.summary: Screen for tuberculosis before starting biologic or other targeted systemic psoriasis therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Screening for tuberculosis is necessary before starting systemic biologic treatment. TNF antibodies such as adalimumab list tuberculosis activation among their adverse events.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An echocardiogram is not the pre-treatment screening the lecture requires.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Radiographs help evaluate arthritis but are not the safety screen required before a biologic.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An ANA is not a required screen before starting a psoriasis biologic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Psoriasis is usually diagnosed clinically; a biopsy is not required before treatment.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has a bright red, sharply bordered eruption with very little scale in both inguinal folds that extends onto the scrotum. He has similar patches in one axilla and the intergluteal cleft. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Psoriasis of the skin folds with scrotal involvement and a sharp border is inverse psoriasis, not tinea cruris.
explanation.whyCorrect: Inverse psoriasis affects intertriginous areas (inguinal, genital, intergluteal, axillary), with less scale and more erythema. Its well-defined border and involvement of the scrotum or vulva distinguish it from tinea cruris, which spares the genitalia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Guttate psoriasis is a shower of small papules on the trunk and proximal limbs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nummular eczema forms coin-shaped patches, not this intertriginous pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seborrheic dermatitis is on the differential, but sharply bordered fold-and-scrotal disease fits the psoriasis variant.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tinea cruris spares the genitalia; involvement of the scrotum argues against it.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with long-standing plaque psoriasis had applied high-potency clobetasol ointment over most of his body for years and stopped abruptly when his supply ran out. Two weeks later his skin is red and scaly from scalp to feet, and he feels chilled. No pustules are present, and he has started no new medications. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Whole-body red, scaly skin after stopping topical steroids in a psoriatic is erythrodermic psoriasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Erythrodermic psoriasis covers the entire skin surface, red and scaly from head to toe. The lecture names withdrawal of topical corticosteroids as a cause; it can be life-threatening with sepsis, respiratory distress, and heart failure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lymphoma is in the erythroderma differential, but the steroid withdrawal history points to psoriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pustular psoriasis features superficial pustules, which are absent; it follows systemic steroid withdrawal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Guttate psoriasis is many small papules, not confluent whole-body redness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Drug-induced erythroderma needs a culprit drug, and he has started none.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with psoriasis plaques on her elbows and knees asks which features of her disease make joint involvement more likely. Which of the following findings most increases her risk of developing psoriatic arthritis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bleeding points when scale is lifted

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lesions at a recent sunburn site

explanation.summary: Nail psoriasis (along with scalp and gluteal cleft disease) raises the risk of psoriatic arthritis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with nail changes have a greater chance of psoriatic arthritis than those without. The lecture also lists scalp and gluteal cleft involvement as raising PsA risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Auspitz sign aids diagnosis but does not predict arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is the Koebner phenomenon, not a stated predictor of arthritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plaque size is not given as a PsA risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Extensor plaques are the typical distribution of plaque psoriasis and are not a stated PsA risk factor.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has had the lesion shown on his elbow for 3 years. It is only mildly itchy. Which diagnosis is most likely?

explanation.summary: A sharply demarcated, salmon-pink plaque covered by silvery-white scale on an extensor surface (the elbow) is classic plaque psoriasis, the most common subtype.
explanation.whyCorrect: Plaque psoriasis favors extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp and low back, with a well-defined border and thick silvery scale over an erythematous base.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lichen simplex chronicus is lichenified, intensely itchy skin from chronic rubbing, without a sharp border or silvery scale.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nummular eczema forms coin-shaped, oozing or crusted itchy patches, not a large plaque with thick silvery scale.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seborrheic dermatitis has greasy yellow scale on the scalp, face and skin folds rather than the extensor elbow.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tinea corporis is an annular plaque with an active scaly border and central clearing, not uniform scale across the plaque.

questions.stem: While examining a patient with a chronic scaly plaque, a clinician gently picks off the scale, producing the appearance shown. Which sign has been elicited?

explanation.summary: Pinpoint bleeding points where psoriatic scale has been removed is the Auspitz sign, which helps separate psoriasis from other scaly diseases that do not bleed when picked.
explanation.whyCorrect: Removing the scale exposes the dilated capillaries in the dermal papillae under a thinned suprapapillary epidermis, which bleed as multiple small points.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Darier sign is urtication and flare after stroking a mastocytosis lesion, not bleeding after scale removal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dermatographism is a raised wheal along a line of stroked skin; there is no bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Koebner phenomenon is new psoriatic lesions appearing at sites of trauma such as scars, not bleeding within an existing plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nikolsky sign is shearing of the epidermis with lateral pressure in blistering diseases such as pemphigus vulgaris.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man has the nail changes shown on several fingers. Because of this nail finding, which condition is he at greatest added risk of developing?

explanation.summary: Nail pitting (with distal onycholysis) is nail psoriasis. Psoriasis of the nails, scalp and gluteal cleft raises the risk of psoriatic arthritis, and nail dystrophy is a CASPAR criterion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Up to 30% of psoriasis patients develop psoriatic arthritis; patients with nail changes are more likely to have it than those without.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative spondyloarthropathy tied to HLA-B27, not specifically predicted by nail pitting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gouty arthritis is crystal arthritis from hyperuricemia; nail pitting does not raise its risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoarthritis is degenerative joint disease unrelated to psoriatic nail changes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rheumatoid arthritis is seropositive and has no link to nail pitting; PsA is characteristically RF-negative.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old with no history of skin disease develops the eruption shown over 1 week, mostly on the trunk and limbs. Which preceding event is most likely?

explanation.summary: A sudden shower of many small (<1 cm) scaly, drop-like papules and plaques in a young person is guttate psoriasis, which typically follows streptococcal pharyngitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Guttate psoriasis is linked to prior group A streptococcal throat infection; amoxicillin is often given, and tonsillectomy can stop recurrent strep-triggered flares.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EBV infection is linked to a morbilliform rash after amoxicillin, not a guttate scaly papular eruption.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Herpes simplex infection triggers erythema multiforme (targetoid lesions), not scaly droplet papules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mycoplasma pneumonia triggers mucositis and erythema multiforme-like eruptions, not guttate psoriasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parvovirus B19 causes slapped-cheek erythema and a lacy reticular rash, not scaly papules.

questions.stem: A punch biopsy is taken from a chronic plaque on the knee of a 45-year-old man. The H&E section is shown. Which diagnosis is most likely?

explanation.summary: Regular acanthosis with evenly elongated rete ridges, confluent parakeratosis, and dilated capillaries in thinned dermal papillae is the classic histology of psoriasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Keratinocyte hyperproliferation driven by the IL-23/Th17 axis gives acanthosis, parakeratosis, loss of the granular layer, elongated rete pegs and dilated papillary vessels (Munro microabscesses may be present).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atopic dermatitis is a spongiotic dermatitis (intercellular edema), without the regular psoriasiform rete elongation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lichen planus shows a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate at the junction, a thickened granular layer and saw-tooth rete ridges.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seborrheic keratosis is an exophytic basaloid proliferation with horn cysts, not elongated rete with parakeratosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Squamous cell carcinoma shows atypical keratinocytes invading the dermis, not orderly, regular rete ridges.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has 3 months of fatigue, joint pain, and a red, sunburn-like eruption across both cheeks and the bridge of the nose that spares the nasolabial folds and eyelids. It worsens after time outdoors. ANA and anti-dsDNA tests are positive. Which of the following best describes this eruption?

explanation.summary: The malar (butterfly) rash sparing the nasolabial folds is acute cutaneous LE, which nearly always signals SLE.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute cutaneous LE is a sunburn-like, photo-distributed rash classically shaped like a butterfly over the cheeks (malar rash) that spares the nasolabial folds and eyelids. Nearly all patients with it have or will develop SLE, and ANA and dsDNA are positive.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Discoid LE produces chronic, scarred, scaly plaques on the face, scalp and ears, not a transient sunburn-like malar rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The heliotrope rash of dermatomyositis is a lilac eruption of the upper eyelids, which this rash spares.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neonatal lupus affects infants exposed to maternal anti-Ro/La antibodies, not a 24-year-old.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SCLE forms annular scaly patches on the V of the chest, back and forearms rather than a butterfly rash on the cheeks.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has several weeks of red, ring-shaped, scaly patches on the V of the chest, upper back, and dorsal forearms. Her physician initially suspected tinea corporis, but a KOH preparation was negative. She has no scarring. Which of the following serum antibodies is most likely to be present?

explanation.summary: Subacute cutaneous LE (annular scaly patches on sun-exposed skin) carries anti-Ro/SS-A in up to 90% of patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Annular, scaly, non-scarring patches on the V of the chest, back and dorsal forearms that mimic tinea or psoriasis are subacute cutaneous LE. Up to 90% of SCLE patients have Ro (SS-A) antibodies, making it the most likely antibody.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-centromere antibodies mark limited scleroderma (CREST), which causes telangiectasias and sclerodactyly, not annular scaly patches.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-Scl-70 is associated with diffuse scleroderma, which causes widespread skin thickening.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-TIF1-gamma marks malignancy-associated dermatomyositis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anticardiolipin antibodies screen for antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, which causes livedo and clots.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman who smokes a pack of cigarettes daily has had scaly plaques on her ears and scalp for 2 years. Older plaques are atrophic and hypopigmented, and the scalp lesions have left patches of permanent hair loss. She has no joint pain, oral ulcers, or systemic symptoms. Which of the following best describes her relationship to systemic lupus erythematosus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About half of patients with this form meet SLE criteria

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nearly all patients with this form have or will develop SLE

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only 10-20% of patients with this form go on to develop SLE

choices.label: D
choices.text: This form develops only after SLE has been diagnosed

choices.label: E
choices.text: This form is unrelated to SLE and never progresses

explanation.summary: Most patients with discoid LE never have SLE; only 10-20% develop it and only about 20% are ANA-positive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic, scarred, scaly plaques of the face, scalp and ears with hypopigmentation and scarring alopecia in a smoker are discoid lupus erythematosus. The majority of DLE patients do not have SLE: only about 20% have a positive ANA and 10-20% develop SLE at some point.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 50% of patients with subacute cutaneous LE, not discoid LE, meet SLE criteria.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Near-universal SLE describes acute cutaneous (malar) LE, not discoid LE.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Most DLE patients never have SLE, so DLE clearly does not require prior SLE.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Discoid LE can progress: 10-20% of patients develop SLE, and 25% of SLE patients have discoid lesions.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has a net-like, violaceous mottling of the skin of both thighs and painful, dusky, necrotic patches on the tips of two toes. She has had a deep vein thrombosis and three unexplained first-trimester pregnancy losses. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to screen for the underlying condition?

explanation.summary: Livedo reticularis, acral necrosis, clots and recurrent miscarriage indicate antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, screened with lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-B2-glycoprotein 1 tests.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antiphospholipid antibody (APLA) syndrome predisposes to venous and arterial clots and obstetric complications; it is often recognized in young women with multiple unexplained miscarriages. Its skin signs are livedo reticularis and acral purpura with necrosis. Screening includes ANA, anticardiolipin antibody, lupus anticoagulant and anti-B2-glycoprotein 1 tests.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-centromere antibodies screen for CREST syndrome, which does not cause clots or miscarriages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Jo-1 marks antisynthetase syndrome (dermatomyositis with interstitial lung disease).
whyWrongByChoice.C: Streptococcal infection is a trigger of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, not of thrombosis with livedo and miscarriage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Aldolase is a muscle enzyme used in dermatomyositis workup.

questions.stem: A newborn girl has a heart rate of 70/min and erythematous annular macules with raised margins on the scalp and around the eyes. ECG shows complete heart block. Her mother is healthy, has no diagnosed autoimmune disease, and is found to carry anti-Ro/SSA antibodies. Which of the following best explains the cardiac finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody blockade of acetylcholine receptors in the sinoatrial node

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody injury and secondary fibrosis of the atrioventricular node

choices.label: C
choices.text: Calcium deposition within the fetal cardiac conduction system

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complex deposition in fetal post-capillary venules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombotic occlusion of fetal coronary arteries by antiphospholipid antibodies

explanation.summary: In neonatal lupus, transferred maternal anti-Ro/La bind apoptotic fetal cardiac cells, causing autoimmune injury and fibrosis of the AV node (heart block).
explanation.whyCorrect: Neonatal lupus results from maternal transfer of anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB antibodies; the mother need not have SLE. The antibodies bind fetal cardiac cells that have undergone physiologic apoptosis during remodeling, causing autoimmune injury and secondary fibrosis of the atrioventricular node and surrounding tissue, which produces heart block that may require permanent pacing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antibodies cause structural injury and fibrosis, not receptor blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Calcium deposition (calcinosis) is a feature of CREST and juvenile dermatomyositis skin, not neonatal heart block.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complexes in post-capillary venules describe leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The responsible antibodies are anti-Ro/La, and the lesion is conduction-system fibrosis, not thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has 2 months of difficulty rising from a chair and combing her hair. Examination shows a lilac eruption of both upper eyelids, scaly violaceous papules over the knuckles, and ragged cuticles. Creatine kinase is elevated. In addition to mammography and chest radiography, which of the following studies is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Dermatomyositis is paraneoplastic in 20-30% of patients, so everyone diagnosed is screened for cancer, including mammography, colonoscopy and chest radiography.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules and proximal muscle weakness establish dermatomyositis. Because 20%-30% of patients develop cancer, all patients are screened by history and physical for breast, lung, GI, ovarian, pancreatic, bladder and throat cancer and receive mammography, colonoscopy and chest radiography. Treating the malignancy is essential to clearing the DM.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Echocardiography is not part of the malignancy screen recommended for dermatomyositis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gottron's papules are a skin finding; hand films add nothing to the cancer screen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The weakness is myopathic; muscle enzymes, biopsy or MRI confirm it, not nerve studies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sinus imaging is not part of the dermatomyositis malignancy screen.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with proximal muscle weakness and a violaceous eruption over his upper back has progressive dyspnea on exertion. His fingers and palms are thickened, scaly, and fissured, and chest CT shows interstitial lung disease. Which of the following antibodies is most likely positive?

explanation.summary: Anti-Jo-1 marks the antisynthetase syndrome: dermatomyositis plus interstitial lung disease and mechanic's hands.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dermatomyositis patients with interstitial lung disease have Jo-1 antibodies, markers of the antisynthetase syndrome, which combines DM, ILD and mechanic's hands (thickened, scaly, fissured digits and palms).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-centromere antibodies mark limited scleroderma (CREST).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-dsDNA is positive in SLE with acute cutaneous lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-Ro is the antibody of subacute cutaneous lupus and neonatal lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TIF1-gamma antibodies mark malignancy-associated dermatomyositis, not lung disease with mechanic's hands.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has 8 months of progressive skin thickening that began in the hands and now involves the arms, trunk, and thighs. Her face appears mask-like, with a beaked nose and narrowed oral aperture. She now has new hypertension and a rising serum creatinine. Which of the following antibodies is most often associated with her condition?

explanation.summary: Diffuse (systemic) scleroderma, with widespread skin thickening and early organ involvement, is associated with anti-Scl-70.
explanation.whyCorrect: Widespread skin thickening, a mask-like face with beaked nose and narrowed mouth, and early kidney involvement describe diffuse (systemic) scleroderma, which progresses early to internal organs (most significantly lungs and kidneys). Anti-Scl-70 autoantibodies are often associated with the diffuse form.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-centromere antibodies are found in limited scleroderma (CREST), where skin involvement stays on the hands, face and neck.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Jo-1 marks the antisynthetase syndrome of dermatomyositis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: La antibodies are seen in subacute cutaneous and neonatal lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TIF1-gamma marks malignancy-associated dermatomyositis.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl has a single firm, smooth, ivory-white plaque on her abdomen with a lilac-colored border. The skin cannot be pinched into wrinkles. She has no Raynaud symptoms, no difficulty swallowing, and normal skin on her hands and face. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Morphea is localized scleroderma: a few circumscribed indurated, ivory-white plaques, sometimes with a violaceous border.
explanation.whyCorrect: The localized form of scleroderma, morphea, presents as a few small to medium plaques of cutaneous sclerosis with circumscribed induration (firm skin that cannot wrinkle), ivory-white hypopigmentation and sometimes a lilac border, without the Raynaud phenomenon or organ involvement of the other forms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Limited scleroderma (CREST) involves the hands, face and neck with Raynaud phenomenon and esophageal dysmotility.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Diffuse scleroderma thickens skin all over the body with early organ involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Discoid LE forms scaly, scarred plaques on the face, scalp and ears rather than a smooth indurated plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gottron's sign is violaceous change over the elbows and knees in dermatomyositis.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with limited scleroderma has episodes in which one or two fingers turn white, then blue, then red after exposure to cold. Warming measures have not prevented the attacks. Which of the following oral medications is most appropriate?

explanation.summary: Raynaud phenomenon is treated with warming, topical nitroglycerin and oral calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Raynaud phenomenon is a heightened vasoconstrictive response to cold or stress causing white (vasoconstriction), blue (cyanosis) and red (reperfusion) phases in one or a few digits. It is treated with warming measures, topical nitroglycerin, and oral calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydroxychloroquine is a first-line treatment for cutaneous lupus, not vasospasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Methotrexate is a treatment for morphea, not for Raynaud attacks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rituximab is used in dermatomyositis, not for digital vasospasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Terbinafine is an antifungal and a common cause of drug-induced SCLE.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man develops many round, 2-4 mm, non-blanching, raised purple papules on his lower legs and buttocks 2 weeks after starting a sulfa antibiotic. His face is spared and the lesions do not itch. A punch biopsy shows neutrophils, nuclear dust, and fibrin in small vessel walls. At which of the following sites are immune complexes deposited?

explanation.summary: Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is caused by immune complexes depositing in post-capillary venules of dependent skin, producing palpable purpura.
explanation.whyCorrect: Drug-induced leukocytoclastic vasculitis (onset 1-3 weeks after beta-lactams, sulfa or NSAIDs) presents as round, non-blanching palpable purpura in dependent areas. IgG, IgM or IgA immune complexes collect along the walls of post-capillary venules in slow-flow areas, and histology shows necrotic venule walls with neutrophils, nuclear dust and fibrin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The deposits in LCV are in vessel walls, not along the epidermal basement membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.B: LCV favors dependent, slow-flow areas, and the face is typically spared.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Medium-vessel involvement brings necrosis and gangrene, which this patient lacks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dilated nail fold capillary loops are a sign of SLE, not the site of LCV.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has crops of raised, non-blanching purpura on her buttocks and legs, colicky abdominal pain, and a swollen, painful knee. Skin biopsy with direct immunofluorescence shows granular IgA deposits in dermal vessel walls. Her purpura is expected to fade within weeks. Which of the following tests are most important for establishing her prognosis, even after the rash resolves?

explanation.summary: In Henoch-Schonlein purpura, creatinine and urinalysis screen for IgA nephritis, which can appear with the purpura or months later.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgA immune complex deposition with palpable purpura, abdominal pain and arthritis in a child is Henoch-Schonlein purpura. Its prognosis depends on the kidney: a creatinine and urinalysis evaluate for renal failure and nephritis (such as blood in the urine), and the nephropathy may appear concomitantly or be delayed several months after the purpura.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ANA and dsDNA evaluate for SLE, which this IgA-mediated syndrome is not.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ANCA-associated vasculitis is independent of immune complexes, unlike this IgA-deposition disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Muscle enzymes are used to evaluate dermatomyositis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These screen for antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has fatigue, joint pain, and the rash shown, which worsened after a beach vacation. Which antibody is most likely present in her serum?

explanation.summary: Butterfly erythema of the cheeks and nasal bridge sparing the nasolabial folds is the malar rash of acute cutaneous lupus; nearly all such patients have SLE, with positive ANA and anti-dsDNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute cutaneous LE is a photosensitive, sunburn-like rash; ANA is uniformly positive and anti-dsDNA is also positive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-centromere antibody marks limited scleroderma (CREST), which shows telangiectasias and sclerodactyly, not a malar rash.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-Jo-1 is a myositis antibody (antisynthetase syndrome), not the marker of acute cutaneous lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Anti-Scl-70 marks diffuse systemic sclerosis, with skin thickening rather than photosensitive malar erythema.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-TIF1-gamma is the dermatomyositis antibody most associated with malignancy; DM affects the eyelids (heliotrope), not a fold-sparing malar pattern.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman who smokes has had several lesions like the one shown for years; the first appeared on her ears and scalp. Which diagnosis is most likely?

explanation.summary: A chronic scarred, atrophic plaque with central depigmentation and a hyperpigmented rim is discoid lupus erythematosus, the scarring form of chronic cutaneous LE that favors the face, scalp and ears.
explanation.whyCorrect: Unlike acute and subacute LE, discoid LE scars; long-standing lesions become hypopigmented, scalp lesions cause scarring alopecia, and smoking is a unique risk factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic plaque psoriasis gives salmon plaques with silvery scale on extensor surfaces and does not leave atrophic, depigmented scars.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertrophic lichen planus forms thick violaceous plaques on the shins, not scarred depigmented plaques on the ears and scalp.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Subacute cutaneous lupus gives annular or psoriasiform patches on the sun-exposed trunk and arms and does not scar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tinea corporis is an annular scaly plaque with central clearing, without scarring or dyspigmentation.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has had the finding shown on her fingers for 2 months. Which associated condition should she be screened for?

explanation.summary: Violaceous scaly papules over the MCP and interphalangeal joints with ragged cuticles are Gottron papules, pathognomonic for dermatomyositis, which is associated with an underlying cancer.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 20-30% of dermatomyositis patients develop cancer (anti-TIF1-gamma has the strongest link), so every patient needs a cancer-directed history and exam plus mammography, colonoscopy and chest imaging.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Celiac disease is linked to dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy extensor vesicles), not Gottron papules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hepatitis C is linked to cryoglobulinemic vasculitis and lichen planus, not dermatomyositis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypothyroidism is not the key association of dermatomyositis; malignancy is.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Latent tuberculosis screening precedes biologic therapy but is not the condition dermatomyositis is classically associated with.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man develops the eruption shown 10 days after starting a new antibiotic. In which vessels are immune complexes most likely deposited?

explanation.summary: Small, round, non-blanching palpable purpura concentrated on dependent areas (legs, feet) is cutaneous small vessel vasculitis, whose histologic correlate is leukocytoclastic vasculitis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In LCV, immune complexes (IgG, IgM or IgA) deposit in post-capillary venule walls in slow-flow dependent skin, giving fibrinoid necrosis, neutrophils and nuclear dust.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Deep dermal arterioles are not the target of LCV; the lesion centers on superficial post-capillary venules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Large elastic arteries are affected in giant cell and Takayasu arteritis, which do not cause palpable purpura.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lymphatic capillaries are not involved in immune complex vasculitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Medium-sized arteries (PAN, ANCA vasculitis) give nodules, livedo, ulcers and necrosis rather than purely round palpable purpura.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old infant has had the rash shown since 2 weeks of age. The mother is healthy. Which maternal antibody most likely caused this?

explanation.summary: Erythematous annular macules with raised margins on the scalp and periorbital skin of an infant are neonatal lupus, caused by transplacental maternal anti-Ro/SSA (and anti-La/SSB) antibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The mother need not have SLE, only the antibodies; the same antibodies can injure the fetal AV node, so the infant needs an ECG to look for congenital heart block.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-centromere antibodies mark limited scleroderma and do not cause neonatal lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-dsDNA is specific for SLE but is not the antibody that crosses the placenta to cause neonatal lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-histone antibodies mark drug-induced lupus, not neonatal lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anti-Smith is highly specific for SLE but is not responsible for neonatal lupus.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has had slowly enlarging, erythematous, scaly plaques on his buttocks and thighs for 6 years. Biopsy shows atypical lymphocytes in the upper dermis and epidermis, and the diagnosis is mycosis fungoides. From which cell are the neoplastic cells most likely derived?

explanation.summary: Mycosis fungoides is a neoplasm of mature, skin-resident CD4+ helper T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cutaneous T cell lymphoma arises from the mature T cells that are part of the skin's resident immune system. In mycosis fungoides the neoplastic cells are thought to derive from CD4+ helper T cells; CD8+ forms exist but are less common.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8+ forms of CTCL exist but are less common; typical MF derives from CD4+ helper cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting cells, not the lymphoid cell of origin of CTCL.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MF is a T-cell neoplasm, not a B-cell neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MF is a neoplasm of mature T cells, not NK cells.

questions.stem: A skin biopsy from a 59-year-old woman with a long-standing annular, scaly patch on the hip shows small, discrete collections of atypical lymphoid cells sitting within the epidermis, with no neutrophils present. What is the name of this histologic finding?

explanation.summary: Intraepidermal clusters of lymphoma cells in MF are called Pautrier microabscesses.
explanation.whyCorrect: In MF, malignant lymphoma cells sometimes invade the epidermis in small clusters, termed Pautrier microabscesses. The name is misleading: true abscesses are collections of neutrophils, whereas these clusters are made of lymphoma cells. They are a unique feature of MF.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Civatte bodies are apoptotic keratinocytes, not collections of atypical lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Spongiform pustules are neutrophilic, unlike the lymphoid clusters described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Munro microabscesses are neutrophil collections in the stratum corneum of psoriasis, not lymphoid clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spongiotic vesicles are fluid collections of eczematous dermatitis, not clusters of atypical lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A pathologist examining a biopsy from a scaly plaque on a 70-year-old man's back notes atypical lymphocytes whose nuclear outlines are deeply folded and indented, resembling the sulci and gyri of the brain. This nuclear appearance is most closely associated with which diagnosis?

explanation.summary: Cerebriform (brain-like, convoluted) nuclei point to mycosis fungoides.
explanation.whyCorrect: The unique feature of MF lymphoma cells is their extremely convoluted nuclear contours, called cerebriform nuclei because the indentations resemble the sulci and gyri of the brain. The term is used almost exclusively with this lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Atopic dermatitis shows a reactive, not atypical, lymphocytic infiltrate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hodgkin lymphoma is not characterized by cerebriform nuclei; the term is used almost exclusively for MF.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Psoriasis is an inflammatory dermatosis without atypical lymphocytes bearing convoluted nuclei.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tinea is a dermatophyte infection; biopsy shows fungal hyphae, not atypical lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man has had itchy, red, scaly patches on his buttocks, lower trunk, and upper thighs for 7 years. Several clinicians diagnosed psoriasis, and topical psoriasis therapies have not helped. Examination shows several thick, scaly, erythematous plaques in these areas. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to establish the diagnosis?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Switch to a stronger psoriasis biologic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whole-body PET scan before any biopsy

explanation.summary: Suspected MF (refractory scaly plaques in covered areas) is confirmed by skin biopsy.
explanation.whyCorrect: MF is a great imitator that is often misdiagnosed for 5-10 years as eczema, tinea or psoriasis. Long-standing scaly plaques in a bathing suit distribution that fail standard therapy should be biopsied; diagnosis rests on recognizing the lesions followed by skin biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Patch testing evaluates allergic contact dermatitis, not a suspected cutaneous lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A KOH scraping looks for fungus; it cannot diagnose a lymphoma that merely mimics tinea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Escalating psoriasis therapy delays the diagnosis; years of failed therapy call for tissue diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Imaging is not the diagnostic step; the diagnosis is made by skin biopsy first.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with mycosis fungoides diagnosed 12 years ago initially had flat, scaly, red lesions on his buttocks. Over the years some became raised and thick. He now has several dome-shaped nodules on his trunk. If his disease continues to progress through the classic clinical sequence, what stage would come next?

explanation.summary: MF stages run patch, plaque, tumor, then erythrodermic.
explanation.whyCorrect: MF progresses through patch, plaque, tumor and then erythrodermic stages. This patient has moved from patches to plaques to tumors; next, the malignant cells can take over the entire skin surface, producing red, scaly skin from head to toe.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypopigmented MF is a clinical variant, not a stage in the progression sequence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The patch stage is the earliest stage; he has already passed it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plaques precede tumors; he has already progressed beyond plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blistering is not one of the classic MF stages.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman has a persistent scaly patch on her flank. Biopsy shows a lymphocytic infiltrate, but histology alone cannot distinguish an inflammatory dermatitis from early mycosis fungoides. Which additional result would most strongly support a neoplastic process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A predominance of neutrophils in the epidermis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single dominant T-cell receptor clone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mixed polyclonal B-cell and T-cell populations

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive fungal hyphae on periodic acid-Schiff stain

explanation.summary: A monoclonal TCR gene rearrangement supports CTCL over a reactive infiltrate.
explanation.whyCorrect: When histology is uncertain, the T-cell receptor gene rearrangement test determines whether the infiltrate is polyclonal (many lineages, as in a reactive process) or monoclonal (one lineage, as in a neoplasm). In CTCL the test often reveals a monoclonal infiltrate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neutrophilic collections are not the lymphoid clusters of MF; MF microabscesses contain lymphoma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A polyclonal infiltrate of many lineages indicates a reactive process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A mixed, polyclonal infiltrate points to a reactive process, not a monoclonal neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hyphae indicate tinea, a mimic of MF, not a lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man is newly diagnosed with patch-stage mycosis fungoides involving 4% of his body surface area. Blood counts and lymph node examination are normal. He asks what this diagnosis means for his life span. Which of the following is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He most likely has a normal life expectancy

choices.label: B
choices.text: He will likely develop pancytopenia within a decade

choices.label: C
choices.text: He will likely progress to internal disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: His disease is curable with a single course of therapy

explanation.summary: Limited cutaneous MF usually carries a normal life expectancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although incurable, MF is usually indolent; most patients control it for years, and most people with limited cutaneous involvement have a normal life expectancy. Follow-up over the years is crucial to monitor for progression in the minority who progress.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Marrow failure is a feature of advanced disease, not the expected course of limited MF.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Progression to internal disease is uncommon; MF stays a skin condition for most patients.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 20-60% 5-year survival describes Sezary syndrome, not limited patch-stage MF.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MF is incurable, although it is usually controllable for years.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with mycosis fungoides. She has a few scaly patches on her buttocks and thighs covering about 5% of her skin surface, with no lymphadenopathy and a normal blood count. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Referral for allogeneic stem cell transplantation

explanation.summary: Limited patch MF is treated first with high-potency topical corticosteroids (with or without topical nitrogen mustard).
explanation.whyCorrect: Mild MF confined to a limited area of skin, which describes most cases, is treated with high-potency topical corticosteroids to minimize inflammation, along with topical chemotherapy such as nitrogen mustard. UVB is used for more stubborn or widespread patches.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Systemic chemotherapy is reserved for disseminated disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MF is not a fungal infection despite its name and its resemblance to tinea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Limited skin-confined MF is managed with skin-directed therapy, usually by dermatologists.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Electron beam radiation is considered for thicker plaques and tumors, not a few limited patches.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old man with patch-stage mycosis fungoides has used high-potency topical corticosteroids twice daily for several months. His patches persist and now cover his trunk, buttocks, and thighs. There are no plaques, tumors, or internal findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?

explanation.summary: Stubborn or widespread patch-stage MF responds to UVB phototherapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: UVB light therapy is a highly effective treatment for more stubborn or widespread patch-stage MF. Radiation is reserved for thicker plaques and tumors, and systemic therapy for disseminated disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Persistent widespread patches warrant escalation to an effective skin-directed therapy now.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antifungals have no role; MF is a lymphoma that only mimics tinea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Systemic chemotherapy is considered only for disseminated disease, which he does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radiation is considered for thicker plaques and tumors, not flat patches.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man has had 2 months of red, peeling, itchy, painful skin covering nearly his entire body, with shaking chills. He had no rash before this, takes no new medications, and has no history of psoriasis or atopic dermatitis. He has diffuse lymphadenopathy. Which finding would best establish the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A monoclonal IgG spike on electrophoresis

choices.label: B
choices.text: A polyclonal T-cell population on flow cytometry

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eosinophilia with a recent drug exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Over 1000 malignant T cells per mL on smear

explanation.summary: Sezary syndrome is defined by circulating malignant T cells (>1000 Sezary cells per mL).
explanation.whyCorrect: Sezary syndrome is a rare, aggressive, leukemic form of CTCL. It differs from MF in that the blood contains malignant T cells (Sezary cells), with more than 1000 per mL on peripheral smear. Erythroderma covering more than 80% of the body is common, and chills reflect disturbed temperature regulation. Most cases arise de novo, without preceding MF.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A paraprotein points to a plasma-cell disorder, not a T-cell neoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A polyclonal population indicates a reactive process, not a T-cell leukemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That suggests DRESS, but he has no new medications.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutrophilic collections suggest psoriasis, which he has no history of.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman has newly diagnosed patch-stage mycosis fungoides affecting about 6% of her body surface area. She has no palpable lymph nodes or organomegaly, and her white blood cell count is normal. Which of the following best describes the role of CT imaging in her staging?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is needed because marrow involvement is common early

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is not needed because it is predicted to be negative

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is required before any topical therapy is started

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the test that confirms the diagnosis of lymphoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: It should be repeated every 3 months for life

explanation.summary: MF with <10% BSA involvement does not need staging imaging.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients presenting with limited body surface area (<10%) do not need imaging for staging, because the tests are predicted to be negative. CT is used when body surface area is high or disease is advanced, to look for lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early disease is confined to the skin; marrow failure is a feature of advanced disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Imaging is unnecessary at <10% BSA; topical therapy can begin without it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The diagnosis is made by skin biopsy, not imaging.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Imaging is not part of routine monitoring of limited disease; follow-up skin exams are.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing mycosis fungoides now has numerous thick plaques and several nodular tumors scattered over her skin. Staging shows no lymph node, blood, or visceral involvement. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Topical antifungal cream to all lesions

explanation.summary: Thick plaques and tumors of MF are treated with radiation, such as total skin electron beam therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Total skin electron beam radiotherapy or targeted radiation therapy is considered for thicker plaques and tumors. Topical agents and UVB treat patches, and systemic chemotherapy is reserved for disseminated disease, which she does not have.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Topical steroids suit mild, limited patches, not numerous thick plaques and tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Systemic chemotherapy is reserved for disseminated disease; hers is skin-confined.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MF is not a fungal infection; antifungals have no role.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tumor-stage disease needs active, effective skin-directed therapy.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man has had this lesion on his buttock and upper thigh for 6 years. Topical antifungals and emollients have not helped. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanation.summary: A large, well-demarcated, reniform (kidney-shaped) erythematous patch in a covered, bathing-suit area that has persisted for years is classic patch-stage mycosis fungoides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycosis fungoides is the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. It begins as slow-growing, circumscribed, scaly patches in covered areas, often annular or reniform, and mimics eczema, tinea and psoriasis for 5-10 years before a biopsy makes the diagnosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Nummular dermatitis (eczema) forms small coin-shaped, often crusted plaques, not a large reniform patch, and responds to emollients and steroids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pityriasis rosea is self-limited over weeks with a herald patch and Christmas-tree pattern, not a 6-year course.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plaque psoriasis favors extensor elbows, knees and scalp with thick silvery scale, not a thin flat patch in a covered site.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tinea corporis has an active scaly advancing border and would have improved with antifungals.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man with a biopsy-proven cutaneous T-cell lymphoma first diagnosed 9 years ago returns for follow-up. His chest is shown. Which clinical stage of mycosis fungoides is present?

explanation.summary: Exophytic, dome-shaped and partly ulcerated nodules arise on a background of flat erythematous patches: this is tumor-stage mycosis fungoides.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycosis fungoides progresses from patches (flat) to plaques (raised) to tumors (nodules of lymphoma cells), and some patients become erythrodermic. The large nodules here mark the tumor stage, which reflects a heavier, diffuse dermal infiltrate and a worse prognosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythroderma is confluent erythema and scale over nearly the entire skin surface, not discrete nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hypopigmented variant shows pale patches, usually in darker skin, without nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Patch-stage lesions are flat; background patches are present, but the nodules indicate more advanced disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plaques are raised and thickened but not exophytic or ulcerated nodules.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear is obtained from a 70-year-old man with intense chills and red, peeling skin over his whole body. Flow cytometry shows loss of CD7. The cell in the center of the image is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: The cell is a lymphocyte with a large, deeply grooved, convoluted cerebriform nucleus: a Sezary cell, the circulating malignant CD4+ helper T cell of Sezary syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma cells derive from CD4+ T cells and have extremely convoluted, brain-like (cerebriform) nuclei. When they circulate they are called Sezary cells; Sezary syndrome is the leukemic form with erythroderma and chills, and flow cytometry shows abnormal T cells lacking markers such as CD7.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Plasma cells have an eccentric round nucleus with clock-face chromatin and a perinuclear hof, not a folded nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Myeloblasts have fine open chromatin, nucleoli and sometimes Auer rods, not a grooved cerebriform nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hairy cells are B cells with abundant cytoplasm and fine hair-like projections; the nucleus is oval, not cerebriform.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactive (viral) lymphocytes have abundant blue cytoplasm that scallops around red cells, with a smooth nucleus.

questions.stem: A skin biopsy is taken from a persistent scaly plaque on the trunk of a 64-year-old man. The circled intraepidermal collection is composed mainly of which cells?

explanation.summary: The circled cluster of dark, irregular lymphoid nuclei inside the epidermis is a Pautrier microabscess, a cluster of malignant T cells unique to mycosis fungoides.
explanation.whyCorrect: In mycosis fungoides the malignant CD4+ T cells home to the epidermis (epidermotropism) and can gather in small intraepidermal clusters called Pautrier microabscesses. The name is misleading: an abscess is made of neutrophils, but these clusters are lymphoma cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acantholytic keratinocytes, which have lost their attachments, appear in pemphigus vulgaris, not as a nest of small dark lymphoid nuclei.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eosinophils and mast cells are not the cells of this cluster; eosinophilic spongiosis is seen in bullous pemphigoid and allergic reactions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Junctional nests of melanocytes are pigmented cells at the dermal-epidermal junction in nevi or melanoma, not a lymphoid cluster.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophil collections in the epidermis are Munro microabscesses of psoriasis; despite the name, Pautrier microabscesses contain no neutrophils.
